raw_response:
I'm 73 this year, and I've been farming these fields in Quzhou for over fifty years. My son works in Shijiazhuang now, so it's mostly me and my wife managing the land. We have five mu of flat land here on the North China Plain. I finished middle school, which was more than most of my generation got, so I can read the labels on fertilizer bags and seed packets well enough, but I learn farming from experience and from watching my neighbors, not from books.

I used to grow cotton too, but I gave that up a few years back. Cotton needs spraying every few days in summer, and at my age I can't carry that sprayer tank up and down the rows anymore. The wheat-maize system is what works for us now. The machines do most of the heavy work. I planted my winter wheat last October with improved seeds from the county supply store—the same kind my neighbors plant. It's reliable and I know how it grows.

Now it's spring, and the wheat is greening up. I will topdress with urea when the weather warms, and I already put down basal compound fertilizer before sowing last autumn. I'll irrigate three times this season: once now for green-up, once at jointing, and once at heading. I'll spray pesticides three times—herbicide, insecticide, and fungicide as the season requires. I rotary-tilled before planting the wheat. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 1000 jin per mu.

After wheat harvest in early June, I will plant hybrid maize seeds the same day. Everyone here uses no-tillage for summer maize now—we just plant directly into the wheat stubble. I'll apply compound fertilizer at planting and topdress with urea at jointing stage. Maize needs two irrigations, one at jointing and one at grain filling. Three pesticide applications should be enough. I don't experiment with new varieties. I buy what the seed store recommends and what has worked for my neighbors. Fertilizer prices are high this year, so I won't waste money, but I won't cut back too much either or the yield will drop.
